title: Do what you can
hookLine: what I forbid, avoid; what I command, do as much as you can
tomorrow: a traveler raises dusty hands to pray. why isn't he answered?

lines: STOP COMPLETELY. WALK AS YOU CAN.
AVOID IT. DO WHAT YOU CAN.
cards: A discharge sheet from a clinic says two things. Stop smoking, completely. And walk every day, as much as you're able.

Nobody calls that unfair. Yesterday's question: why avoid all of the wrong, but only some of the right? Abu Hurayrah reports a line from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, built exactly like that sheet.
What I have forbidden you, avoid it. What I have commanded you, do of it as much as you can. On paper, it's lopsided.

teach.b: Here's the answer commentators give. Leaving something is in everyone's reach: not doing a thing takes no strength, no money, no health. Doing takes all of those, and people have different amounts of each.
So the forbidden is avoided entirely, and the commanded is done as far as your strength goes.
The Qur'an says it in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Now the story behind the line, from Sahih Muslim. The Prophet tells the people Hajj has been made due on them.
A man asks: every year? The Prophet says nothing. The man asks again, and a third time.
Then: if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you couldn't have done it. Leave me be as long as I leave you be.
Then come the lines about avoiding and doing, and a warning that people before them were ruined by too many questions and by disagreeing with their prophets.
One to tell a friend tonight: even the avoiding has mercy in it. The Qur'an allows forbidden food to someone forced by hunger.
The religion was given at a size people could carry, and the man's extra question could only have made it heavier.

how: Islamic law builds ability into its rules: someone who can't stand prays sitting, the sick and travelers may delay a fast, and Hajj is due only on those able to make it.

games.q: what does “do what you can” mean?
o: do as much of the good as you are able
do only the parts that feel easy today
do one big good deed instead of many

games.q: avoid, and do what you can — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith asks the same all-out effort for every command
do of it as much as you can. it's the forbidden that's avoided entirely.
the line came after a man kept asking if Hajj was due every year
'if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you couldn't have done it.'
'do what you can' means do whatever is convenient
it means as far as your strength goes: a real amount, measured by ability, not mood.

games.q: your grandmother can't stand through the prayer anymore and feels bad about sitting. what fits today's hadith?
o: pray sitting: the command is done as much as she's able.
skip prayer until she's strong enough to stand again.
keep standing even when it hurts, or it won't count.
games.why: a report in Sahih al-Bukhari says it plainly: pray standing; if you can't, sitting; if you can't, on your side. as much as you can.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing you've been putting off because you can't do all of it. Do the smallest real piece that's within reach right now: one line of the message, one page, one corner of the room.
Then sit back for the rest of the time, and let that piece count as what it is.

wordCard.voice: Do what you can: the commanded, done as far as your strength reaches, and the forbidden, left entirely. Nobody is tasked beyond their scope.

orig.note: Arabic: do of it what you are able.

carryVoice: Worth repeating today: as much as you can, and that's a real amount, never a zero. Eleven days into year five.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7288; Sahih Muslim 1337 (Abu Hurayrah: what I forbid, avoid; what I command, do as much as you can; the question 'every year?' about Hajj)

sources.q: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:173 (forbidden food allowed to one compelled by necessity)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (Imran ibn Husayn: pray standing; if unable, sitting; if unable, on your side)
